definition: Collusion means a secret agreement to act together dishonestly.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word collusion. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know collusion should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Skaters began whispering about collusion when two judges' scores matched to the decimal, event after event, all season long.
Teamwork is open, honest coordination; collusion borrows the cooperation but hides it and points it at something dishonest.
Conspiracy goes beyond collusion: colluding firms secretly rig a market they still operate in, while conspirators plot an entire scheme—often a crime—from start to finish.

Connivance is quietly letting wrongdoing happen — the guard who sees the theft and looks the other way. Collusion is more active: the parties secretly agree and work the dishonest scheme together. A conniver permits what others do; collusion means doing it as partners.

Complicity is being involved in someone else's wrongdoing — by helping, by knowing, or by staying silent — and it requires no agreement. Collusion needs more: a secret pact, usually between supposed rivals, to act together dishonestly. One person can be complicit alone; collusion takes coordinated partners.

At the regional esports final, two supposedly rival teams played out a semifinal they had privately scripted weeks earlier, having agreed to split the prize money no matter who advanced.
When the chat logs surfaced, the league voided the match and named the offense: collusion.
Collusion is sharper than 'cheating' because it names a secret, dishonest partnership—usually between parties who are supposed to be competing—so the deceit lies in the cooperation itself.
Collusion belongs to news reports, courtrooms, and rulebooks: it accuses supposed rivals of secretly working as one.
For an open joint effort, say cooperation or teamwork; for a full secret plot, conspiracy.
Collusion pairs naturally with words like 'evidence,' 'investigation,' and 'between.'

In 1877, two railroads competed for the grain traffic out of Prairie Junction, and their newspapers traded insults all summer.
Farmers noticed something the papers did not: whenever one line raised its freight rate, the other raised its own within the week, to the penny.
A young clerk finally compared the two companies' rate books and found the pages had been drafted in the same hand.
The 'rival' presidents, it emerged, had been meeting quietly in a Chicago hotel for years, dividing the harvest between them and setting rates together.
The public feud, a judge later wrote, was the costume; the collusion underneath it was the business.
